title: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar and John Dewey: Pragmatism, Education, and Moral Democracy
summary: At Columbia University in New York (1913–1916), young Bhimrao Ambedkar absorbed the democratic pragmatism of philosopher John Dewey, forging his lifelong philosophy of social emancipation.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 158: நேருவும் விழுந்த செய்தியாளரும்: “அப்படியானால் நாமும் எழுந்துவிடலாம்”
full_text:
Between 1913 and 1916, inside the Low Memorial Library at Columbia University in New York, a solitary young scholar from India could be found at the desks from early dawn until closing time.

His name was Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar. Having traveled abroad on a scholarship provided by the Maharaja of Baroda, Ambedkar pursued economics, sociology, and philosophy with ferocious hunger, attending the lectures of America's renowned philosopher of democracy, John Dewey.

Observing his relentless routine, Professor Dewey once paused by his desk and asked with paternal concern:
"Bhimrao, your classmates spend their evenings enjoying the cultural sights of New York, yet you study eighteen hours a day in this quiet hall. Do your eyes never tire of print?"

Ambedkar looked up, his expression burning with profound mission:
"Professor Dewey, my fellow students are preparing for comfortable careers, but behind me stand millions of my oppressed brothers and sisters in India who have been denied the right to literacy, water, and human dignity for two thousand years!
I have not crossed the oceans merely to earn academic titles. I am here to forge the intellectual armor needed to liberate my people. From your lectures, I have learned that genuine democracy is not a mechanical government structure; it is an associated mode of living governed by moral communication and mutual respect. Until my people are free, I have no time for leisure!"

Dewey was deeply moved, later referring to Ambedkar as one of the finest minds he had ever instructed. Ambedkar turned education into the supreme instrument of civil rights.
